newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian government embroiled in share storm.
newsitem.headline: Australian government embroiled in share storm.

text.p: A political storm over ministerial behaviour threatened to engulf the Australian government on Wednesday as the opposition targeted more senior ministers over their shareholdings.
Two junior members of the conservative government resigned earlier this week, saying they had taken ministerial decisions that could be seen to benefit companies in which they held shares.

On Wednesday the Labor opposition widened its attack from embattled Industry Minister John Moore, under fire for his stake in a venture capital company, to Finance Minister John Fahey and even Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer.

"Two men have gone because they were in technical breach of the guidelines, not because they have done anything dishonest," Prime Minister John Howard said on radio. "And now an attempt is being made to sort of smear the whole of my government."
Howard himself set tough guidelines when his Liberal-National coalition swept to power in March, ending 13 years of Labor Party rule.
Ministers were not to own shares in companies with interests in their own portfolios, he announced earlier this year.
But the opposition discovered last week that Assistant Treasurer Short, responsible for banking, held shares in one of the big Australian banks.
Short quit on Sunday. Brian Gibson, the parliamentary secretary to the treasurer, followed on Tuesday, telling parliament a conflict of interest left him no honourable course.
It was the opposition's first successful offensive against the new government, which has appeared untouchable since the election.
On Wednesday it emerged that Fischer had held shares in the Broken Hill Proprietary Ltd (BHP) while his duties as trade minister required him to promote the company's interests overseas.
Howard said he was satisfied Fischer had done nothing wrong, but the opposition said his own policy demanded action.
"You're the one who issued the guidelines, Prime Minister," opposition industry spokesman Simon Crean told him in parliament.
But Howard said the affair would go no further.
"I certainly don't expect another resignation," he told reporters.
"But I've asked my colleagues to attend very carefully to their affairs and I believe they will and they have, and I await question time with great interest."
Besides, he proposed that ministers should be able to invest through blind trusts, which would prevent them knowing exactly which shares they owned.
But opposition leader Kim Beazley said he was trying to change the rules to protect his ministers retrospectively.
"This is a classic, this little suggestion of the prime minister's," Beazley told reporters. "You can't get the ministers to fit the guidelines so you make the guidelines fit the ministers."

The Australian Financial Review reported that Fahey had failed to declare ownership of shares registered in his name. Fahey said he had sold the shares years ago, but the buyer had failed to register the transfer.
Moore's venture-capital company invests in other companies that have interests in government industry policy.
He says he is trying to sell the shares but since the company is so small there is no effective market for them.
